title: RNA-seq for Graves' orbitopathy, Graves' disease and health control
description: This study investigates the molecular landscape of Graves’ disease (GD) and its extrathyroidal manifestation, Graves’ orbitopathy (GO), with a specific focus on the systemic impact of thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor (TSHR) signaling. While GD and GO are primarily characterized by peripheral autoimmunity, emerging evidence suggests these conditions involve neuroimmune crosstalk and central nervous system (CNS) alterations.  To bridge the gap between peripheral autoimmunity and central involvement, we performed bulk RNA sequencing on peripheral blood samples from a cohort including 20 Graves’ orbitopathy patients, 20 Graves’ disease patients (without orbitopathy), and 20 healthy controls.  Our analysis identifies TSHR as a critical molecular hub mediating interactions between peripheral immune cells and the CNS. By comparing the transcriptomic signatures across these three groups, we aim to characterize the systemic immune dysregulation unique to GO and GD.

samples.title: GDPBMC001
samples.description: Protocols: Graves’ Disease (GD) Group: Patients were diagnosed based on clinical and biochemical evidence of hyperthyroidism, including elevated free triiodothyronine (FT_3) and free thyroxine (FT_4), suppressed thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) levels, and the presence of TSH receptor antibodies (TRAb). Inclusion required a definitive diagnosis of GD without clinical evidence of orbitopathy.Graves’ Orbitopathy (GO) Group: Patients met the diagnostic criteria for GD and presented with clinical manifestations of orbitopathy as defined by the EUGOGO (European Group on Graves' Orbitopathy) guidelines. Active GO was assessed using the Clinical Activity Score (CAS), with a score of 3/7 or 4/10 indicating active inflammation.Healthy Control (HC) Group: Age- and sex-matched volunteers with no history of thyroid dysfunction, autoimmune diseases, or systemic inflammatory conditions. All HC subjects exhibited normal thyroid function tests (FT_3, FT_4, and TSH) and were negative for thyroid autoantibodies.All venous blood samples (10 mL) were collected in the morning after an overnight fast. Samples were processed within 2 hours to isolate Peripheral Blood Mononuclear Cells (PBMCs) via Ficoll-Paque density gradient centrifugation. Isolated cells were resuspendend in RNAlater or immediately frozen at -80. Total RNA was extracted from the samples using the TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen, USA) or the RNeasy Mini Kit (Qiagen, Germany) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. To remove potential genomic DNA contamination, an on-column DNase I treatment was performed. The concentration and purity of the extracted RNA were quantified using a NanoDrop 2000 spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). RNA integrity was further assessed using the Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer (Agilent Technologies); only samples with an RNA Integrity Number (RIN) > 7.0 and a 28S/18S ratio > 1.5 were proceeded to library construction. Sequencing libraries were prepared using a strand-specific protocol optimized for the MGI platform. The process included mRNA enrichment, fragmentation, cDNA synthesis, and adapter ligation using indexing compatible with DNBseq technology.
